summary: A tribute written in the style of a story, remembering Jon Postel, the long-time IANA leader who died in 1998. It is a personal memorial written by Vint Cerf and not a technical specification.

eli5.summary: This is a loving story about the man who for years kept the internet's lists of numbers and names in order, written after he passed away.

subtitle: A tribute to Jon Postel, the Internet's keeper of numbers

tldr.problem: In October 1998, Jon Postel, the founding IANA director who had served the Internet for 30 years, died. The community needed to remember his contributions.
tldr.mechanism: Vint Cerf (then chairman of the Internet Society) wrote an emotional remembrance describing Postel's role in creating the Internet, his integrity, and his legacy, and proposed the Jonathan B. Postel Service Award in his memory.
tldr.outcome: An acknowledgment of one individual's outsized contribution to the Internet. Postel left behind the RFC Editor role, the IANA function, and institutions that continue his work today.

today: RFC 2468 is a historical document and memorial. The Jonathan B. Postel Service Award exists and is awarded annually to individuals with long-standing contributions to the Internet community.

sections.title: Who Was Jon Postel
sections.content:
Jon Postel was present at the Internet's creation. He worked under Professor Leonard Kleinrock at UCLA on the ARPANET, the predecessor to the Internet. When Steve Crocker proposed the Request for Comments series to document the emerging protocols, Postel became the instant RFC Editor. Later, when the Internet needed someone to keep track of protocol numbers, host assignments, and domain names, Postel became the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA).

For nearly 30 years, Postel was the living memory and the principled arbiter of the Internet's namespace. He was private but intensely engaged, known among friends for his loyalty and for his willingness to fight for what was right in technical debates.
sections.eli5: Jon kept lists of who got which numbers and names for the whole Internet, and he wrote down the rules everyone agreed on. He did this job better than anyone could have, for thirty years.

sections.title: His Contributions to the Internet
sections.content:
RFC 2468 enumerates Postel's roles: founder of the Internet Architecture Board, first individual member of the Internet Society (he and Steve Wolff raced to apply), trustee of the Internet Society, custodian of the .US domain, founder of Los Nettos Internet, and director of the networking research division at USC Information Sciences Institute. Beyond these titles, he edited the first RFC Editor manual and championed both the technical and the poetic in Internet documentation.

Vint Cerf notes that Postel inspired loyalty among colleagues and personified selfless service. He took little in return for his work, though he received the ITU's Silver Medal (an award usually reserved for heads of state) late in his life.
sections.eli5: Jon started the groups that make rules for the Internet. He made sure documents were clear and fair. He quietly did the hardest work and let other people take credit.

sections.title: What He Left Behind
sections.content:
RFC 2468 emphasizes that Postel's legacy lives in the institutions and procedures he created. The IANA function continues under a successor. The RFC series and the systematic documentation of Internet standards continue. The Internet Architecture Board and the Internet Society, which he helped found, carry forward his vision.

Cerf concludes by proposing the Jonathan B. Postel Service Award to recognize long-standing service to the Internet community, and pledges that Postel be its first recipient posthumously.
sections.eli5: The groups and systems Jon built are still here, still following the careful and honest ways he taught them. His name is now on a prize given to people who serve the Internet quietly over many years.
